calendar.gloss_nfp_short: The number of new jobs created in the US non-farm sector. Released the first Friday of every month.
calendar.gloss_nfp_full: One of the key labor market indicators. A beat strengthens the dollar and raises expectations of a Fed rate hike. A weak NFP pressures the USD and raises the odds of monetary easing.
calendar.gloss_cpi_short: The Consumer Price Index. The main US inflation gauge (calculated by the BLS).
calendar.gloss_cpi_full: Measures the change in prices for a consumer basket of goods. Core CPI excludes the volatile food and energy components. Above forecast → dollar strength. Below forecast → dollar weakness, expectations of a Fed pause.
calendar.gloss_ppi_short: The Producer Price Index. A leading signal for consumer-level inflation.
calendar.gloss_ppi_full: Reflects the change in prices producers receive for finished goods. Often viewed as an early indicator of pressure on CPI. Rising PPI while CPI lags signals future inflation.
calendar.gloss_pce_short: The Fed's preferred inflation gauge. Accounts for actual consumer behavior.
calendar.gloss_pce_full: Core PCE (ex food and energy) is the Fed's key target (2% goal). Unlike CPI, it flexibly accounts for shifts in consumption patterns. Published with the personal income/spending report (BEA).
calendar.gloss_gdp_short: Gross Domestic Product — the total value of all goods and services produced in a country.
calendar.gloss_gdp_full: Released in three estimates: advance → second → final. Strong GDP growth confirms economic resilience and supports the national currency. Two consecutive quarters of negative GDP growth constitute a technical recession.
calendar.gloss_pmi_mfg_short: Shows business sentiment among purchasing managers in industry. Threshold: 50.
calendar.gloss_pmi_mfg_full: A reading above 50 means expansion in the manufacturing sector, below 50 means contraction. The final S&P/Markit PMI is released early in the month; ISM Manufacturing is typically released on the first business day of the month.
calendar.gloss_pmi_svc_short: The services-sector equivalent of PMI. Threshold: 50. More significant for the US (services make up ~70% of GDP).
calendar.gloss_pmi_svc_full: Since the services sector makes up most of GDP in developed economies, PMI Services is often more important than PMI Manufacturing. A sustained reading above 55 signals an overheating economy.
calendar.gloss_ism_short: The American equivalent of PMI, from ISM. Threshold: 50. Manufacturing and services data are released monthly.
calendar.gloss_ism_full: ISM Manufacturing is considered more relevant than S&P PMI for the US market. The "new orders" component is watched especially closely by traders as a leading signal.
calendar.gloss_unemployment_short: The share of unemployed people in the labor force. Released alongside NFP.
calendar.gloss_unemployment_full: Rising unemployment pressures the dollar, falling unemployment supports it. The Fed targets a rate of roughly 4–4.5% (nominal "full employment"). High unemployment makes a rate cut more likely.
calendar.gloss_jobless_claims_short: Weekly data on first-time unemployment benefit claims. Released every Thursday.
calendar.gloss_jobless_claims_full: A leading labor-market indicator. Rising claims signal weakening employment. Sensitive to holidays and seasonal factors. Levels above 300k are seen by the market as an alarming signal.
calendar.gloss_continuing_claims_short: The number of people continuing to receive unemployment benefits. Released weekly.
calendar.gloss_continuing_claims_full: Released with a one-week lag relative to initial claims. A sustained rise indicates the unemployed are taking longer to find work — a negative signal for the dollar.
calendar.gloss_jolts_term: JOLTS — Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey
calendar.gloss_jolts_short: The number of job openings in the US economy. A key measure of labor supply-demand balance.
calendar.gloss_jolts_full: The Fed uses JOLTS to gauge overheating in the labor market. When job openings significantly exceed the number of unemployed, it signals inflationary pressure from wages.
calendar.gloss_adp_short: ADP's estimate of the change in private-sector employment. Released 2 days before NFP.
calendar.gloss_adp_full: Often viewed as a preview of the official NFP. Its correlation with the official report is moderate, so the market reacts more cautiously than to NFP.
calendar.gloss_retail_sales_short: The change in retail trade sales volume. A measure of consumer activity.
calendar.gloss_retail_sales_full: Consumption accounts for ~70% of US GDP, so retail sales are a key indicator of economic activity. A beat supports the dollar. Core Retail Sales excludes autos as the most volatile component.
calendar.gloss_fomc_short: A meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee. They announce the rate decision and publish a statement.
calendar.gloss_fomc_full: 8 scheduled meetings per year. Besides the rate itself, what matters is the accompanying statement, the dot plot, and the Fed chair's press conference. A hawkish tone (hinting at a hike) strengthens the USD; a dovish one (easing) weakens it.
calendar.gloss_eia_crude_short: The weekly change in US crude oil inventories (U.S. Energy Information Administration). Released on Wednesdays.
calendar.gloss_eia_crude_full: Rising inventories → oversupply → pressure on oil prices. Falling inventories → shortage → oil price gains. The API publishes preliminary data on Tuesday evening as an early indicator.
calendar.gloss_eia_gas_short: The weekly change in US natural gas storage. Released on Thursdays.
calendar.gloss_eia_gas_full: Important for trading natural gas (NG=F). Seasonality: storage draws are normal in winter. An abnormally large draw at the peak of heating season → rising gas prices.
calendar.gloss_durable_goods_short: The change in new orders for goods with a useful life of more than 3 years.
calendar.gloss_durable_goods_full: A leading indicator of manufacturing activity and corporate investment. Core Durable Goods (ex aircraft and transportation) is more stable and better reflects underlying trends.
calendar.gloss_trade_balance_short: The difference between a country's exports and imports of goods and services.
calendar.gloss_trade_balance_full: A trade deficit (imports > exports) creates demand for foreign currency, putting pressure on the exchange rate. A surplus does the opposite. For the USD, the balance with China, Japan, and the EU is especially significant.
calendar.gloss_housing_starts_short: The number of housing starts and building permits issued.
calendar.gloss_housing_starts_full: A leading indicator of the housing market's health. Building permits are released at the same time and are often more important, since they reflect future activity. Sensitive to mortgage rates.
calendar.gloss_home_sales_short: The number of purchase transactions in the US secondary housing market.
calendar.gloss_home_sales_full: The secondary housing market is significantly larger than the primary one. Sales are sensitive to mortgage rates: rising rates slow the market. The NAR publishes data monthly.
calendar.gloss_consumer_confidence_short: The Conference Board's Consumer Confidence Index. Reflects the public's assessment of the current and future economy.
calendar.gloss_consumer_confidence_full: Released on the last Tuesday of the month. Consists of two components: Current Situation and Expectations. Used as a leading indicator of consumer spending.
calendar.gloss_michigan_short: The University of Michigan's Consumer Sentiment Index. Two releases per month: preliminary and final.
calendar.gloss_michigan_full: The preliminary reading is released mid-month, the final one at month-end. The 5-year inflation expectations component is watched especially closely by the market and the Fed.
calendar.gloss_factory_orders_short: Factory Orders: new orders for manufactured goods. Industrial Production: output volume.
calendar.gloss_factory_orders_full: Industrial Production + Capacity Utilization are released together by the Fed. High capacity utilization (>80%) signals possible inflationary pressure. Factory Orders is a broader measure that includes services.
calendar.gloss_challenger_short: The number of announced layoffs, from Challenger, Gray & Christmas.
calendar.gloss_challenger_full: Released monthly on the first Thursday. Rising layoffs are an early warning sign for the labor market. The market's reaction is relatively muted, but the data matters for NFP context.

chart.explain_main_tpl: The price is {where} {name} {price} — a level where price has historically reversed.

chart.hint_pivots: Pivots — support/resistance levels calculated from the highs and lows of previous periods. Green — support (S1, S2), red — resistance (R1, R2), gold — the pivot point (PP).
chart.hint_patterns: Patterns — notable candlestick formations over the last 40 bars. ↑ green arrow — bullish signal (hammer, bullish engulfing, etc.), ↓ red — bearish (harami, bearish engulfing, etc.), ● yellow — neutral (doji). Context, not a trade signal.
chart.hint_smc: SMC — market structure: HH (Higher High) — a new high above the previous one, uptrend; HL (Higher Low) — the pullback doesn't break the previous low, uptrend; LH (Lower High) — a high below the previous one, weakness; LL (Lower Low) — a new low, downtrend. BOS — break of structure (confirmation); OB — Order Block, a zone of large orders; FVG — a liquidity gap that price often fills.

eduglossary.subtitle: Key trading terms and macroeconomic indicators. Use the search or category filter.
eduglossary.term.leverage.name: Leverage
eduglossary.term.ath.def: All-Time High — the highest price an asset has ever reached.
eduglossary.term.bear-market.def: A market decline of 20%+ from a recent high.
eduglossary.term.bull-market.def: A market rally of 20%+ from a recent low.
eduglossary.term.volatility-vix.def: A measure of price uncertainty. The VIX is the S&P 500's "fear index."
eduglossary.term.long-short.def: Long — a bet on a rise. Short — a bet on a decline.
eduglossary.term.stoploss.def: An order that closes a position once a loss threshold is reached.
eduglossary.term.takeprofit.def: An order that locks in profit once a target is reached.
eduglossary.term.leverage.def: Trading with borrowed funds. Amplifies both profit and loss.
eduglossary.term.liquidity.def: How easily an asset can be bought/sold without moving its price.
eduglossary.term.hedge.def: A position taken to offset the risk of another position.
eduglossary.term.spread.def: The difference between the buy price (ask) and the sell price (bid).
eduglossary.term.flashcrash.def: A sudden price drop over a short period, often followed by a recovery.
eduglossary.term.bos.def: A break of market structure — evidence of a trend change or continuation.
eduglossary.term.orderblock.def: An institutional zone of interest, where a large player entered a position.
eduglossary.term.fvg.def: A price inefficiency — a gap between candles that the market often returns to.
eduglossary.term.rsi.def: Relative Strength Index — an oscillator ranging from 0–100. Overbought (>70) and oversold (<30) zones.
eduglossary.term.macd.def: Moving Average Convergence Divergence — the difference between two EMAs plus a signal line.
eduglossary.term.atr.def: Average True Range — a measure of volatility.
eduglossary.term.fib-levels.def: Retracement levels of 23.6%, 38.2%, 50%, 61.8% — support/resistance zones within a trend.
eduglossary.term.liquidity-sweep.def: Price moving beyond a key level to "sweep" stop orders before reversing.
eduglossary.term.pmi-manufacturing.name: PMI Manufacturing — Business Activity Index (Manufacturing)
eduglossary.term.pmi-services.name: PMI Services — Business Activity Index (Services)
eduglossary.term.unemployment-rate.name: Unemployment Rate
eduglossary.term.continuing-claims.name: Continuing Claims
eduglossary.term.retail-sales.name: Retail Sales
eduglossary.term.fomc.name: FOMC — Fed Interest Rate Decision
eduglossary.term.durable-goods.name: Durable Goods Orders
eduglossary.term.nfp.def: The number of new jobs created in the US non-farm sector. Released the first Friday of every month. A beat strengthens the USD and raises expectations of a Fed rate hike.
eduglossary.term.cpi.def: The Consumer Price Index. The main US inflation gauge (calculated by the BLS). Core CPI excludes food and energy. Above forecast → dollar strength.
eduglossary.term.ppi.def: The Producer Price Index. Reflects the change in wholesale prices — a leading signal of pressure on CPI. Rising PPI usually precedes rising consumer inflation.
eduglossary.term.pce.def: The Fed's preferred inflation gauge. Core PCE (ex food and energy) is the Fed's key target (2% goal). Accounts for actual shifts in consumption patterns.
eduglossary.term.gdp.def: Gross Domestic Product. Released in three estimates: advance → second → final. Two consecutive quarters of negative growth constitute a technical recession.
eduglossary.term.pmi-manufacturing.def: Shows purchasing managers' sentiment in industry. Threshold: 50. Above means expansion, below means contraction. ISM Manufacturing is an alternative version released by the American ISM.
eduglossary.term.pmi-services.def: The services-sector equivalent of PMI. Threshold: 50. More significant for the US (services make up ~70% of GDP). A sustained reading above 55 signals an overheating economy.
eduglossary.term.ism.def: American business-climate indices from ISM, covering manufacturing and services. The "new orders" component is a leading signal. ISM Manufacturing is released on the first business day of the month.
eduglossary.term.unemployment-rate.def: The share of unemployed people in the labor force. Published alongside NFP. The Fed targets a rate of roughly 4–4.5% (nominal "full employment").
Weekly data on first-time unemployment benefit claims (every Thursday). A rise above 300k is an alarming signal for the labor market.
eduglossary.term.continuing-claims.def: The number of people continuing to receive unemployment benefits. Released weekly, with a lag. A sustained rise indicates the unemployed are finding it harder to get new work.
eduglossary.term.jolts.def: The number of open job vacancies in the US economy (Job Openings and Labor Turnover Survey). The Fed uses it to gauge overheating in the labor market. Vacancies >> unemployed → inflationary pressure.
eduglossary.term.adp.def: ADP's estimate of the change in private-sector employment. Published 2 days before NFP as a preview. Its correlation with NFP is moderate.
eduglossary.term.retail-sales.def: The change in retail trade sales volume. A measure of consumer activity (~70% of US GDP). Core Retail Sales excludes autos. Above forecast → dollar support.
eduglossary.term.fomc.def: A meeting of the Federal Open Market Committee. 8 scheduled meetings per year. Besides the rate, the dot plot and the Fed chair's press conference matter. A hawkish tone → USD strength.
eduglossary.term.eia-crude.def: The weekly change in US crude oil inventories (Wednesdays). Rising inventories → pressure on oil. A drawdown → higher prices. The API publishes preliminary data on Tuesday evening.
eduglossary.term.eia-natgas.def: The weekly change in US natural gas storage (Thursdays). An abnormal drawdown during heating season → higher gas prices.
eduglossary.term.durable-goods.def: The change in new orders for goods with a useful life of more than 3 years. Core Durable Goods (ex aircraft) better reflects underlying trends in corporate investment.
eduglossary.term.trade-balance.def: The difference between exports and imports of goods and services. A sustained deficit creates demand for foreign currency and pressures the exchange rate. For the USD, the balance with China, the EU, and Japan matters most.
eduglossary.term.housing-starts.def: Housing Starts — the number of new construction starts. Building Permits — permits issued (a leading indicator of future construction). Both are sensitive to mortgage rates.
eduglossary.term.home-sales.def: The number of purchase transactions in the secondary housing market. The secondary market is significantly larger than the primary one. A decline as mortgage rates rise is a standard signal.
eduglossary.term.consumer-confidence.def: The Conference Board's Consumer Confidence Index. Released on the last Tuesday of the month. Consists of an assessment of the current situation and expectations — a leading indicator of spending.
eduglossary.term.michigan-sentiment.def: The University of Michigan's Consumer Sentiment Index. Two releases per month. The 5-year inflation expectations component is closely watched by the Fed.
eduglossary.term.factory-orders.def: Factory Orders: new orders for manufactured goods. Industrial Production + Capacity Utilization (from the Fed): output volume and factory utilization. Utilization >80% is an inflation risk.
eduglossary.term.challenger-cuts.def: The number of announced layoffs (Challenger, Gray & Christmas). Released on the first Thursday of the month. An early signal of possible labor-market weakening ahead of NFP.

chart.thermo_range_hint: How wide today's range (high−low) is compared to the last 60 days. Above the 50th percentile — a wider move than usual, below — calmer than usual. Click for history.
chart.thermo_news_hint: How many times more or less news there is about this instrument today versus a normal day. ×1.0 — normal, higher — elevated media/social attention. Click for history.
chart.thermo_event_hint: The nearest major economic release or speech that could move the price sharply. Click to see how this instrument reacted to this event in the past.
chart.thermo_dvol_hint: Implied volatility (the market's expectation of future move size) over the last 90 days. Above the 50th percentile — the market is pricing in sharper moves than usual.
chart.thermo_zone_hint: Distance in points to the nearest "attention zone" — a price range where price has historically reversed most often (shown as gold lines on the chart). The closer price gets to the zone, the higher the chance of a reaction.
chart.thermo_zone_hint_empty: No significant reversal zones found near the current price.
chart.thermo_range_hist_caption: Each bar is one day's range (high−low). Taller — the day was more volatile. The gold bar on the right is today.
chart.thermo_dvol_hist_caption: Each bar is one day's implied volatility. Taller — the market was pricing in sharper moves. The gold bar on the right is today.
chart.thermo_news_hist_caption: Recent publications about this instrument — their count drives the "News backdrop" score. Headlines are from their original sources, usually in English.
chart.event_card_caption: An economic release that could move the price. Forecast/Prev. — the expected and previous value of the indicator.
